title: Measuring the Brain: First Principles
summary: Learn the physics, signal processing and experimental logic that every neuroscience recording and imaging method depends on.

lessons.title: Scales of the Brain: Molecules to Behavior and the Tools for Each

levels.kid:
Your brain is like a giant city. From an airplane, you see the whole city. Zoom in, and you see neighborhoods, then houses, then people, then the tiny tools in their hands.

The brain works the same way. Tiny pieces called **molecules** build cells called **neurons**. Neurons link up into teams called **circuits**. Circuits make up brain areas. All the areas working together let you walk, talk and dream.

Scientists need a different tool for each zoom level. A super microscope can see molecules. A thin wire can listen to one neuron. A big scanner can watch the whole brain at once.

No single tool sees everything. Each tool is best at one zoom level. So scientists use many tools together, like detectives sharing clues.
levels.hs:
Neuroscience works across a huge range of **scales**. A single ion channel is about 10 nanometers wide. The gap between two neurons, the **synaptic cleft**, is about 20 nanometers. A neuron's cell body is about 10 to 30 micrometers across. The whole human brain holds roughly **86 billion neurons** and around **100 trillion synapses**, and it weighs about 1.4 kilograms. Time spans just as much: a channel can open in under a millisecond, a nerve impulse lasts about 1 millisecond, and learning can take days or years.

Scientists often describe a ladder of levels:
- **Molecules**: ion channels, receptors, neurotransmitters
- **Synapses**: connections between neurons
- **Neurons**: single cells that send electrical signals
- **Circuits**: groups of connected neurons doing a job
- **Brain regions and systems**: areas like the hippocampus or motor cortex
- **Behavior**: what the whole animal does

Every tool has a **spatial resolution**, the smallest detail it can separate, and a **temporal resolution**, how quickly it can follow changes. Compare two human methods. **EEG** uses electrodes on the scalp and tracks electrical changes within milliseconds, but it blurs activity over centimeters. **fMRI** measures changes in blood oxygenation. It builds images from small 3D cubes called **voxels**, usually a few millimeters across, but blood responds slowly, over several seconds. No tool wins at everything, so scientists combine them.
levels.college:
Each level of brain organization has characteristic sizes and timescales, and the tools that study it are chosen to match.

- **Molecules (angstroms to nanometers; microseconds to milliseconds)**: channel and receptor structures are solved by **X-ray crystallography** and **cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM)**, which now reaches near-atomic resolution of around 2 to 3 angstroms. Single-channel patch clamp records the opening of one protein in real time.
- **Synapses (tens of nanometers to about 1 micrometer)**: electron microscopy resolves the 20 nm cleft and vesicles about 40 nm wide; patch clamp measures synaptic currents lasting milliseconds.
- **Neurons (micrometers, with axons reaching far longer)**: whole-cell patch clamp captures voltage inside one cell; extracellular electrodes detect spikes from outside.
- **Circuits (hundreds of micrometers to millimeters)**: **two-photon microscopy** with genetically encoded calcium indicators such as **GCaMP** images thousands of neurons; **Neuropixels** probes record hundreds of neurons at once along a 1 cm shank.
- **Regions and whole brain (millimeters to about 15 cm; milliseconds to minutes)**: EEG, MEG, fMRI and PET.
- **Behavior (seconds to years)**: video tracking, task performance, clinical testing.

Three tradeoffs shape every choice:
- **Resolution** in space and time
- **Coverage**: how much of the brain is sampled at once
- **Invasiveness**: whether surgery, genetic modification or radiation is needed

High-resolution methods usually see a small patch and need invasive access. That is why single-neuron recordings in humans happen mainly during clinically necessary surgery.

Many methods measure a **proxy**, not electrical activity itself. GCaMP fluoresces when calcium enters a neuron after spikes, so it reports calcium rather than membrane voltage. fMRI's **BOLD** (blood-oxygen-level-dependent) signal reflects blood flow and oxygen changes triggered by neural activity, peaking about 4 to 6 seconds later. PET follows radioactive tracers over minutes. Knowing what each signal physically represents, and at what scale, is the first step to interpreting it correctly.
levels.phd:
Churchland and Sejnowski's 1988 Science review made the scale problem visual. They plotted each technique by the logarithm of the spatial range it covers against the logarithm of its temporal range. The nervous system spans roughly nine orders of magnitude in space, from ion channel pores to the whole brain, and more than ten in time, from submillisecond gating to lifelong plasticity. Their plot exposed gaps, notably the **mesoscale** between single units and whole-region imaging, that two-photon imaging and dense electrode arrays later began to fill.

**Marr's three levels** (computational, algorithmic, implementational) add a conceptual axis. A mechanism at one physical scale can implement an algorithm described at another, and explanations do not always reduce cleanly downward.

Connectomics shows what bottom-up mapping costs:
- *C. elegans*: 302 neurons, reconstructed by White and colleagues in 1986.
- Adult *Drosophila* (FlyWire, 2024): about 140,000 neurons and roughly 50 million synapses.
- Human temporal cortex (Shapson-Coe et al., 2024): 1 cubic millimeter containing about 57,000 cells and 150 million synapses, producing about 1.4 petabytes of data.

Cross-scale interpretation is where nuance lives. Logothetis and colleagues (2001) recorded electrophysiology simultaneously with fMRI in macaque visual cortex. BOLD was better predicted by **local field potentials** than by spiking, suggesting it reflects synaptic input and local processing more than output firing. EEG and MEG face the **inverse problem**: infinitely many source configurations produce identical scalp fields, so localization depends on modeling assumptions. Calcium indicators act as a slow filter on spiking. GCaMP transients decay over hundreds of milliseconds, and single isolated spikes may fall below detection, which biases estimates toward active cells. Extracellular electrodes favor large, frequently firing neurons, leaving quiet cells as a kind of neural dark matter.

Jonas and Kording (2017) applied lesions, tuning curves, connectomics and other standard analyses to a simulated MOS 6502 microprocessor running classic video games. The analyses produced neuroscience-like findings, yet they failed to reveal how the chip actually computed. The study is a warning that rich data at one scale do not by themselves yield mechanism.
levels.expert:
For a clinician-scientist, scale is practical: the neurosurgical workflow already crosses it. Before resecting a tumor near eloquent cortex, task fMRI and diffusion tractography map regions and white-matter tracts at millimeter scale. In the operating room, **electrocorticography (ECoG)** records population activity from the cortical surface. **Direct cortical stimulation**, descended from Penfield's awake-craniotomy mapping, tests whether a site is essential for speech or movement. During deep brain stimulation surgery, **microelectrode recording** resolves single units, and the subthalamic nucleus is recognized partly by its dense, irregular firing and beta-band activity. Each step trades spatial precision, coverage and risk.

Pitfalls when moving between scales:
- **Reverse inference** (Poldrack, 2006): concluding a mental process occurred because a region activated is weak when that region activates in many tasks.
- **Ecological fallacy**: a signal averaged over a voxel or electrode need not describe any individual neuron, and opposing cell types can cancel.
- **Preoperative fMRI is not ground truth**: altered neurovascular coupling near gliomas can suppress BOLD, so intraoperative stimulation remains the reference standard for eloquent mapping.
- **Mismatched timescales**: a seconds-long hemodynamic signal cannot resolve the order of millisecond events.

Recent advances are narrowing gaps. Neuropixels probes adapted for humans (Paulk et al., 2022) recorded hundreds of single units intraoperatively. The MICrONS consortium (2025) linked two-photon functional imaging to an electron-microscopy reconstruction of about a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex, joining activity and wiring in the same cells. BRAIN Initiative cell atlases built from single-cell transcriptomics have catalogued thousands of molecularly defined cell types in mouse and human brains, adding a molecular axis to anatomical scale.

Open questions remain. Scaling the 1.4-petabyte cubic millimeter to a whole human brain implies on the order of a zettabyte of EM data. Which fine-scale details matter for behavior, and which average away, is unknown. Whether the mesoscale has its own lawful dynamics or simply summarizes micro events is actively debated. The working strategy is multimodal: pair methods whose blind spots differ, and validate proxies against direct measurements whenever possible.

keyPoints: The brain spans molecules (nm, microseconds) to behavior (whole body, years)
Human brain: about 86 billion neurons and around 100 trillion synapses
Every tool trades spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage and invasiveness
EEG is fast but spatially blurry; fMRI is sharper in space but slow
Many signals are proxies: GCaMP reports calcium, BOLD reports blood oxygenation
Bridging scales needs multiple methods whose blind spots differ

test.q: Which human method tracks brain activity within milliseconds but blurs it over centimeters?

test.explain: fMRI's BOLD signal reflects blood flow and oxygen changes triggered by neural activity. Magnetic fields from synaptic currents are measured by MEG.

How safe a tool is for a patient
The smallest detail a tool can see
How fast a tool follows a change

test.q: A GCaMP signal in a neuron most directly reflects:

test.q: Neuropixels probes are notable because they:

Map ion channel structure in tissue
Record hundreds of neurons at once

test.q: What two-word term describes how quickly a tool can follow changes in brain activity?
test.explain: Temporal resolution is about speed. EEG has excellent temporal resolution, while fMRI is limited by slow blood responses.

test.q: The gap between two neurons where signals pass, about 20 nanometers wide, is the synaptic ___.
test.explain: The synaptic cleft is about 20 nm wide, small enough that electron microscopy is needed to see it.

test.q: An fMRI image is built from small 3D cubes, usually a few millimeters across, called ___.
test.explain: A voxel is a volume pixel. Each one averages the activity of many thousands of neurons.

kidTest.q: What are brain cells called?

kidTest.q: Which tool can listen to just one neuron?
kidTest.explain: A thin wire placed very close can pick up one neuron. A big scanner watches the whole brain instead.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists use many different tools?
choices: Each scientist likes a different one
Each tool is best at one zoom level
Old tools wear out very quickly
kidTest.explain: Some tools see tiny molecules and some see the whole brain, so scientists combine them.

kidTest.q: Neurons link up into teams. What are these teams called?
kidTest.explain: Teams of connected neurons are called circuits. Molecules are much smaller pieces.

kidTest.q: Tiny building pieces that make up cells are called m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ s.

advancedTest.q: Logothetis and colleagues found BOLD was better predicted by local field potentials than by spiking. What does this imply about a BOLD increase?
choices: It proves projection neurons raised their firing rates
It means blood flow changes faster than synapses
It reflects synaptic input more than spiking output
It shows glia produce most of the BOLD signal
advancedTest.explain: LFPs largely reflect synaptic and local processing, so BOLD can rise without a matching increase in output spiking. It does not prove projection neurons fired more.

advancedTest.q: Why can't EEG pinpoint a brain source from scalp recordings alone?
choices: Scalp electrodes sample too slowly for brain rhythms
Many source arrangements give the same scalp pattern
EEG mainly detects deep subcortical action potentials
Skull conductivity is identical to that of the cortex
advancedTest.explain: This is the inverse problem: infinitely many source configurations can produce the same scalp field, so localization depends on modeling assumptions. EEG is fast, so speed is not the issue.

advancedTest.q: Standard neuroscience analyses applied to a simulated microprocessor failed to reveal how it worked. The main lesson is that:
choices: Rich data alone do not yield mechanistic insight
Microprocessors share no principles with brains
Lesion studies outperform any recording method
Recording more units would have solved the chip
advancedTest.explain: Jonas and Kording showed that lesions, tuning curves and connectomics gave neuroscience-like results without explaining the computation. Data at one scale are not the same as understanding mechanism.

advancedTest.q: A two-photon GCaMP study labels a neuron 'silent' during a task. What is the best caution?
choices: Calcium signals lag spikes by several seconds
The indicator may miss single or sparse spikes
Two-photon imaging mostly records glial activity
The neuron was probably damaged by the laser
advancedTest.explain: GCaMP filters spiking, and isolated spikes can fall below detection, which biases results toward active cells. Its transients decay over hundreds of milliseconds, not seconds of lag.

lessons.title: Electricity for Neuroscientists: Voltage, Current, Resistance and Ohm's Law

levels.kid:
Think about water in a garden hose. The water pressure is the **push**. The water that comes out is the **flow**. If you squeeze the hose, it gets harder for water to get through. That squeeze is called **resistance**.

Electricity works the same way. The push is called **voltage**. The flow is called **current**. Anything that slows the flow down is **resistance**.

Your brain cells are tiny electric machines! Instead of water, they move tiny bits of salt that carry electric charge. These bits are called **ions**. Ions slip in and out through little doors in the cell's skin called **channels**.

One simple rule ties it all together. More push makes more flow. More resistance makes less flow. Scientists call this rule **Ohm's law**, and they use it to listen to brain cells.
levels.hs:
Neurons are electrical, so every recording method rests on three quantities.

- **Voltage** (V, measured in volts) is the difference in electrical potential energy per unit of charge between two points. It is the "push" on charges. Neurons work in millivolts (mV). A typical resting neuron sits near −70 mV, meaning the inside is 70 thousandths of a volt more negative than the outside. That number is the **membrane potential**.
- **Current** (I, measured in amperes, A) is the rate at which charge flows. In neurons, charge is carried by **ions** such as sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻), not by free electrons as in a copper wire. Neural currents are tiny: picoamperes (pA, trillionths of an amp) to nanoamperes (nA).
- **Resistance** (R, measured in ohms, Ω) is how strongly something opposes current. Its reciprocal, **conductance** (g = 1/R), measured in siemens (S), describes how easily current flows. Open ion channels act as conductances.

**Ohm's law** connects them: **V = I × R**.

A real example: a scientist injects 100 pA into a neuron whose **input resistance** is 200 megaohms (MΩ). The voltage changes by 100 × 10⁻¹² A × 200 × 10⁶ Ω = 0.02 V, or 20 mV. That is enough to bring many neurons close to firing. Small neurons usually have higher input resistance, so the same current moves their voltage further.
levels.college:
Neurophysiology is circuit analysis applied to living tissue. The core quantities have typical working scales:
- Voltage: membrane potentials span roughly −100 to +60 mV.
- Current: single channels pass about 0.5-20 pA. Whole cells pass pA to tens of nA.
- Resistance: neuron input resistances range from tens of MΩ (large pyramidal cells) to over 1 GΩ (small cells such as cerebellar granule cells).

**Sign conventions.** Membrane potential (Vm) is defined as inside minus outside. Membrane current is positive when positive charge leaves the cell (outward) and negative when it enters (inward). Inward cation current, like Na⁺ entry, is plotted as a negative deflection and depolarizes the cell.

**Conductance and driving force.** Each ion species has a **reversal potential** (E) at which its net flux is zero, because its concentration gradient exactly balances the electrical gradient. Ohm's law for one ion becomes **I_ion = g_ion × (Vm − E_ion)**. The term (Vm − E_ion) is the **driving force**. At rest (Vm ≈ −70 mV), with E_Na ≈ +55 mV, Na⁺ has a large inward driving force. With E_K ≈ −90 mV, K⁺ has a small outward one.

Worked example: a channel with a 20 pS conductance and a 100 mV driving force passes 20 × 10⁻¹² S × 0.1 V = 2 pA.

**Kirchhoff's laws.** Currents entering a node sum to zero (current law), and voltages around a closed loop sum to zero (voltage law). At a steady resting potential the net membrane current is zero, even though K⁺, Na⁺ and other ions keep flowing. The inward and outward currents simply cancel.

**Series and parallel.** Resistances in series add; conductances in parallel add. Every open channel is a conductance in parallel with all the others, so opening more channels lowers the cell's input resistance. Measuring input resistance (inject a small current step, then divide the steady voltage change by it) gives a quick readout of how many channels are open.
levels.phd:
**Counting charge.** One ampere is one coulomb per second, and the elementary charge is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so 1 pA corresponds to about 6.2 million monovalent ions per second. A 2 pA single-channel current is roughly 12 million ions per second. Currents this small explain why resolving single proteins required new technique: Neher and Sakmann's single-channel recordings (1976), made routine by the gigaseal (Hamill et al., 1981), earned the 1991 Nobel Prize.

**The parallel-conductance model.** Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) represented each ionic pathway as a battery (E_ion) in series with a conductance, with all pathways in parallel across the membrane. Setting net current to zero gives the steady-state potential **Vm = Σ g_i E_i / Σ g_i**, a conductance-weighted average of reversal potentials. This is why the resting potential sits near E_K, because K⁺ leak dominates, but not exactly at it.

**Ohm's law is a local approximation.** Ion permeation is not intrinsically linear. The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz current equation predicts curved I-V relations when concentrations differ across the membrane. Ca²⁺, with a roughly 10,000-fold gradient, carries almost no outward current. Channels add their own nonlinearities. Kir channels show **inward rectification** because intracellular Mg²⁺ and polyamines (such as spermine) plug the pore on depolarization. NMDA receptors are blocked by extracellular Mg²⁺ at negative potentials. Hence two definitions: **chord conductance**, I/(V − E), and **slope conductance**, dI/dV. These can even differ in sign, as in the NMDA negative-slope region.

**Shunting inhibition.** When E_Cl lies near Vm, opening GABA_A receptors produces little voltage change yet inhibits strongly. The added conductance lowers input resistance, so a given excitatory current yields a smaller depolarization (ΔV = I × R_in), while Vm is held toward E_Cl.

**Tissue is a resistor too.** Extracellular space acts as a volume conductor with a resistivity of roughly 3 Ω·m in cortex. For a point current source in a homogeneous medium, potential falls off as V = I/(4πσr), where σ is conductivity. This Ohmic relation underlies field potentials and current-source density analysis. How much tissue capacitance and anisotropy distort it remains debated.
levels.expert:
At the bench and the bedside, Ohm's law mostly appears as error budgets.

**Series resistance.** In whole-cell voltage clamp, current flows through the pipette tip and residual membrane, the access or series resistance (Rs, often 5-20 MΩ). The cell sits away from the command potential by I × Rs: 2 nA through 15 MΩ is a 30 mV error, enough to badly distort activation curves of large sodium currents. Remedies include low-resistance pipettes, amplifier Rs compensation (commonly 70-80%), shrinking currents by partial ion substitution or lower temperature, and reporting Rs with the data.

**Seal leak as a voltage divider.** Seal resistance sits in parallel with the cell. With a 1 GΩ seal on a cell whose true input resistance is 3 GΩ, you measure 0.75 GΩ. Because the seal leak is nonselective and reverses near 0 mV, the recorded resting potential is also depolarized. This error is worst for small, high-resistance neurons, and for sharp microelectrodes, whose impalement leak makes cells look leakier and more depolarized than in patch recordings.

**Liquid junction potential.** Different ion mobilities in pipette solution and bath create an offset, roughly 10-15 mV with potassium gluconate internals, that makes true Vm more negative than the reading unless corrected.

**In vivo conductance states.** Under intense synaptic bombardment, cortical neurons in vivo can show input resistance several-fold lower than in slices (Destexhe's "high-conductance state"), changing how any current translates into voltage.

**Dynamic clamp** (Sharp; Robinson and Kawai; both 1993) uses I = g(V − E) directly: a computer reads Vm, calculates the current an artificial conductance would pass, and injects it in real time, adding or subtracting virtual channels.

**Clinical translation.** Deep brain stimulation generators run in constant-voltage or constant-current mode. Under constant voltage, delivered current varies inversely with electrode impedance, which shifts over the first weeks to months as the electrode-tissue interface matures. Impedance checks also catch hardware faults: very high values suggest an open circuit such as a lead fracture, very low values a short. Electrode impedance is frequency-dependent, so calling it resistance is a simplification.

Open question: how well single-compartment Ohmic estimates describe dendrites that are electrically distant from the soma.

keyPoints: Voltage is the push, current is the flow of charge, resistance opposes flow
Ohm's law: V = I × R; conductance g = 1/R, measured in siemens
In neurons, current is carried by ions, not free electrons
Ion current = conductance × driving force (Vm − reversal potential)
Opening channels adds parallel conductance and lowers input resistance
Series resistance and seal leak are Ohm's-law errors in recordings

test.q: Which equation is Ohm's law?
test.explain: Voltage equals current times resistance. Rearranged, I = V/R, so higher resistance means less current for the same voltage.

test.q: What is electrical conductance?
choices: The product of voltage and current
The speed of a moving ion
test.explain: Conductance g = 1/R and describes how easily current flows. Stored charge relates to capacitance, a different property.

test.q: You inject 50 pA into a neuron with an input resistance of 400 MΩ. How much does its voltage change?
test.explain: V = I × R = 50 × 10⁻¹² A × 400 × 10⁶ Ω = 0.02 V, which is 20 mV.

test.q: By convention, the membrane potential is defined as:
test.explain: Vm is inside relative to outside, which is why a resting neuron reads about −70 mV: its inside is more negative.

test.q: The driving force on an ion is equal to:
test.explain: Driving force is (Vm − E_ion). Ion current equals conductance times this driving force.

test.q: Under standard conventions, an inward flow of positive ions such as Na⁺ is:
test.explain: Inward cation current is negative by convention, and bringing positive charge in makes the inside less negative, which is depolarization.

test.q: Two neurons receive the same injected current. Neuron A has double the input resistance of neuron B. Neuron A's voltage change is:
test.explain: By V = I × R, with I fixed, voltage change scales with resistance, so doubling R doubles the voltage change.

test.q: At a steady resting potential, the net current across the membrane is:
choices: Equal to the sodium current alone
test.explain: Kirchhoff's current law: at steady state, inward and outward ion currents cancel, so net current is zero even though individual ions keep moving.

test.q: A channel has a conductance of 20 pS and a driving force of 100 mV. What current does it pass?
test.explain: I = g × driving force = 20 × 10⁻¹² S × 0.1 V = 2 × 10⁻¹² A, or 2 pA.

test.q: What unit is used to measure conductance, the reciprocal of resistance?
test.explain: Conductance is measured in siemens (S); single channels are usually in picosiemens (pS).

test.q: In neurons, electric current is carried by charged atoms called ___, not by free electrons.
test.explain: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ carry neural currents, unlike the electrons that carry current in metal wires.

test.q: Resistance is measured in units called ___.
test.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω); neuron input resistances are often in megaohms or gigaohms.

kidTest.q: In the garden hose story, what is voltage like?
kidTest.explain: Voltage is the push that makes charge move, like water pressure.

kidTest.q: What is electric current?
kidTest.explain: Current is the flow, like the water coming out of the hose.

kidTest.q: If you squeeze a hose, which one goes up?
kidTest.explain: Squeezing makes it harder for water to get through. That is more resistance, so less flows.

kidTest.q: What are the little doors that ions use to go in and out of brain cells?
kidTest.explain: Channels are tiny doors in the cell's skin that let ions through.

kidTest.q: Brain cells move tiny charged bits of salt called i _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Ions are the charged particles that carry electricity in your brain.

advancedTest.q: GABA_A receptors open while E_Cl sits almost exactly at the resting potential, so Vm barely moves, yet the neuron fires less. Why?
choices: It cuts input resistance, so EPSPs shrink by Ohm's law
It drives the membrane far toward the potassium reversal
It directly blocks sodium channels in the initial segment
It raises input resistance, so excitatory charge leaks away
advancedTest.explain: Shunting inhibition adds parallel conductance, lowering R_in, so the same excitatory current produces a smaller depolarization. Raising R_in would do the opposite.

advancedTest.q: You patch a small neuron with a true input resistance of 3 GΩ, but your seal is only 1 GΩ. What will you most likely record?
choices: About 0.75 GΩ, with Vm depolarized toward 0 mV
About 4 GΩ, with Vm hyperpolarized toward E_K
About 3 GΩ, with Vm unchanged by the seal
About 0.75 GΩ, with Vm hyperpolarized toward E_K
advancedTest.explain: Seal and cell are in parallel: 1 × 3 / (1 + 3) = 0.75 GΩ. The nonselective seal leak reverses near 0 mV, pulling the recorded resting potential depolarized.

advancedTest.q: In whole-cell voltage clamp, a 2 nA sodium current flows through an uncompensated series resistance of 15 MΩ. What is the consequence?
choices: ~30 pA error in the recorded current
~30 mV gap between command and true Vm
~300 mV error that would rupture the seal
~3 mV error, negligible for most I-V work
advancedTest.explain: Voltage error = I × Rs = 2 × 10⁻⁹ A × 15 × 10⁶ Ω = 0.03 V. The cell is 30 mV off the command, which distorts activation curves.

advancedTest.q: With E_K = −90 mV, a K⁺ channel passes large inward current at −120 mV but almost no outward current at −60 mV, though both driving forces are 30 mV. Best interpretation?
choices: Voltage-dependent pore block lowers g with depolarization
Outward potassium flow is offset by chloride influx
E_K shifts toward zero during each depolarizing step
The driving forces differ, so Ohm's law still explains it
advancedTest.explain: This is inward rectification: intracellular Mg²⁺ and polyamines plug Kir channels on depolarization, so conductance itself is voltage-dependent and the I-V relation is non-Ohmic.

lessons.title: The Neuronal Membrane as an RC Circuit

levels.kid:
Every brain cell, called a neuron, has a thin skin around it. Scientists like to picture that skin as a bucket with a few tiny holes.

When charge (tiny bits of electricity) flows into the cell, it's like pouring water into the bucket. The bucket wall holds the water in. In electronics, a part that stores charge like this is called a **capacitor**.

The tiny holes are **ion channels**. They let some water leak out. A part that lets charge leak slowly is called a **resistor**.

The bucket has to fill up, so the cell's voltage does not jump up all at once. It rises gradually. If you stop pouring, the water slowly leaks back out. Fewer holes means the bucket holds its water for longer.
levels.hs:
Your neurons run on electricity, and engineers have a simple way to describe them: as an **RC circuit**, a circuit made of a resistor (R) and a capacitor (C).

- **Capacitor**: two conductors separated by a thin insulator. The cell membrane is a fatty lipid bilayer only about 4-5 nanometres thick, with salty, conducting fluid on both sides. That makes it a capacitor that stores charge. Its capacitance is about 1 microfarad per square centimetre.
- **Resistor**: ion channels let charged ions such as K+ and Na+ cross the membrane. The fewer channels are open, the higher the **membrane resistance**.
- **Battery**: each ion has a **reversal potential**, the voltage at which it stops flowing overall. These act like batteries in the circuit.

The resistor and capacitor sit side by side (in parallel), and that has an important result: voltage changes take time. Injected current first has to charge the capacitor, so the voltage rises along a curve instead of jumping instantly. The **time constant**, written τ (tau), equals R × C. After one τ, the voltage has reached about 63% of its final value. In many neurons τ is 10 to 30 milliseconds.

Example: two signals reach a neuron 5 ms apart, and its τ is 20 ms. The first signal hasn't faded yet when the second arrives, so they add up. This is called **temporal summation**.
levels.college:
The **equivalent circuit** of a patch of membrane has three elements in parallel branches:
- **Membrane capacitance (Cm)**: the ~4-5 nm hydrophobic bilayer separates two electrolyte solutions. Specific capacitance is close to 1 µF/cm² and roughly constant across cell types, because bilayer thickness and dielectric constant are similar.
- **Membrane resistance (Rm)**, or its inverse, conductance (g = 1/R): set by open ion channels. Specific membrane resistance varies widely, from about 1,000 to over 50,000 Ω·cm².
- **Batteries (E_ion)**: each ion's reversal potential, given by the Nernst equation, in series with that ion's conductance.

**Charging.** Current through the capacitor is I_C = C·dV/dt, so it flows only while voltage is changing. Ionic current is I_ion = g(V − E). For a current step I, voltage follows V(t) = I·R(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with τ = RmCm. At t = τ the response is 63% complete, and after about 3τ it is ~95%. When the step ends, the voltage decays along a mirror-image exponential.

**Why τ is size-independent but input resistance is not.** τ is the product of specific resistance (Ω·cm²) and specific capacitance (F/cm²), so area cancels out. **Input resistance** (R_in = ΔV/ΔI) does fall as area grows, because more membrane means more channels in parallel. Small neurons such as cerebellar granule cells can have input resistances near a gigaohm, so a few picoamps shift their voltage a lot. Large motor neurons have far lower values.

**Functional consequences:**
- **Low-pass filtering**: fast fluctuations are smoothed, with a corner frequency of 1/(2πτ), about 8 Hz for τ = 20 ms.
- **Temporal summation**: inputs arriving within roughly one τ add together.
- **Tiny charge, big voltage**: Q = CV, so changing 1 cm² of membrane by 100 mV needs only 10⁻⁷ coulombs. An action potential therefore barely changes bulk ion concentrations.

Opening channels lowers R and shortens τ, so the cell's state changes how it integrates input.
levels.phd:
The RC description comes from impedance measurements by **Cole and Curtis (1939)**. They found squid axon capacitance near 1 µF/cm², and they showed that membrane conductance rose sharply during the action potential while capacitance stayed nearly constant. **Hodgkin and Huxley (1952)** built this into their equivalent circuit: a capacitor in parallel with Na+, K+ and leak branches, each a conductance in series with its battery:

C dV/dt = −Σ g_i(V − E_i) + I_inj

Setting dV/dt = 0 gives the **chord conductance equation**, V_ss = Σ g_iE_i / Σ g_i. The steady-state voltage is a conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials. The membrane sits closest to the battery with the largest conductance, which is why rest lies near E_K.

The capacitance value has since been refined. **Gentet, Stuart and Clements (2000)** measured about 0.9 µF/cm² in nucleated patches from cortical neurons, which removed the geometric uncertainty of whole-cell estimates.

**Lapicque (1907)** modelled nerve as a leaky capacitor that fires when it reaches threshold. This is the ancestor of today's **leaky integrate-and-fire** neuron, τ dV/dt = −(V − E_L) + R·I. It captures the strength-duration relation: brief stimuli need more current because the capacitor must charge before leakage wins.

A single RC compartment is accurate only for electrically compact cells. Extended dendrites and axons are distributed RC networks, described by **cable theory** (Hodgkin and Rushton, 1946; Rall from the late 1950s). The **length constant** λ = √(d·Rm / 4Ri) sets how far a steady voltage spreads before decaying to 37%, where d is diameter and Ri is axial resistivity. Charging transients in such cells are sums of exponentials. Rall's 'peeling' method separates the slowest component (τ0 ≈ τm) from faster equalizing components that reflect electrotonic length.

Nuances:
- Rm is not truly constant. HCN (Ih) and other voltage-dependent channels make 'passive' parameters voltage-dependent, so τ is measured with small steps and sometimes with channel blockers.
- In vivo, synaptic bombardment produces a **high-conductance state** (Destexhe, Paré and colleagues). It can lower input resistance several-fold and shorten τ to a few milliseconds, which sharpens temporal precision.
- Myelin stacks many membranes in series. This divides capacitance and multiplies resistance per unit length of internode.
levels.expert:
For anyone who will patch neurons or stimulate them in an operating room, the RC model is a working tool, not just a diagram.

**The membrane test.** In whole-cell recording, a small voltage step produces a current spike that decays exponentially. Integrating the transient gives Cm; a typical pyramidal neuron has a whole-cell capacitance of tens to a few hundred picofarads. The peak and decay give the access, or **series resistance (Rs)**. The clamp is itself an RC circuit: voltage at the membrane settles with τ ≈ Rs·Cm. With 10 MΩ access onto 100 pF, that is 1 ms, too slow to clamp fast Na+ currents faithfully. Rs also causes voltage errors proportional to current. Amplifier compensation helps, but overcompensation makes the clamp oscillate.

**Space clamp.** In cells with long dendrites, a somatic electrode cannot hold distal membrane at the command voltage because of cable filtering. Distal synaptic currents appear smaller and slower, and kinetics measured at the soma can be badly distorted (Williams and Mitchell, 2008).

**Capacitance as a readout.** Membrane area sets Cm, so vesicle fusion adds measurable capacitance. **Neher and Marty (1982)** used this to track exocytosis in chromaffin cells. The approach can now resolve single-vesicle fusion and endocytosis.

**Clinical stimulation.** The strength-duration curve is described by two values. **Rheobase** is the minimum current for very long pulses. **Chronaxie** is the pulse duration needed at twice rheobase. Large myelinated axons have short chronaxies, roughly tens to a couple of hundred microseconds, while somata and dendrites have longer ones. Short pulse widths in deep brain stimulation and intraoperative mapping therefore favour activating axons. In demyelination, exposed internodal membrane adds capacitance and leak. Charge is shunted away from the next node, and conduction can fail.

**Open questions.**
- **Eyal and colleagues (2016)** reported specific capacitance near 0.5 µF/cm² in human cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, which would allow faster signal transfer. Other measurements find values nearer 0.9-1 µF/cm², and the issue is still debated.
- Fitting passive models is degenerate. Different combinations of Rm, Ri and Cm can reproduce the same transients, especially when the morphology from reconstructions is uncertain.

keyPoints: The lipid bilayer is a capacitor (~1 µF/cm²); ion channels are resistors; reversal potentials are batteries
Capacitive current flows only while voltage changes: I = C·dV/dt
Time constant τ = Rm·Cm; voltage reaches ~63% of its final value after one τ
τ is independent of cell size, but input resistance falls as membrane area grows
The RC membrane low-pass filters input and enables temporal summation
Steady-state voltage is a conductance-weighted average of reversal potentials

test.q: In the RC model of a neuron, the lipid bilayer behaves as:
test.explain: The thin insulating bilayer separates two conducting salt solutions, which is the structure of a capacitor. Ion channels, not the bilayer, provide resistance.

test.q: In the equivalent circuit, open ion channels are represented by:
test.explain: Channels let ions flow across the membrane, so they act as resistors (conductances). More open channels means lower membrane resistance.

test.q: The membrane time constant τ is equal to:
test.explain: τ = Rm × Cm. Raising either resistance or capacitance slows how quickly the membrane voltage changes.

test.q: After one time constant of a steady current step, the voltage has reached about what fraction of its final value?
test.explain: 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.63. 37% is the fraction left during a decay after one τ, and ~95% is reached after about 3τ.

test.q: Typical specific capacitance of a neuronal membrane is:
test.explain: Bilayer capacitance is close to 1 microfarad per square centimetre, refined to about 0.9 µF/cm² in careful measurements.

test.q: Why does a large neuron have lower input resistance than a small one?
choices: Its lipid membrane is much thicker
Its ions travel more slowly inside
It has more channels in parallel
test.explain: More membrane area means more channels in parallel, which lowers total resistance. A larger cell actually has more total capacitance, not less.

test.q: Because of its RC properties, the membrane acts as a:
test.explain: The capacitor smooths fast fluctuations and passes slow changes, which is low-pass filtering with a corner frequency of 1/(2πτ).

test.q: Compared with a neuron that has a short time constant, a neuron with a longer time constant will:
choices: Lose its resting potential more quickly
Need much more charge per millivolt change
Sum inputs that arrive further apart
test.explain: A slower decay means an earlier input is still present when a later one arrives, so inputs spread further apart in time can still summate.

test.q: Current flows through the membrane capacitance when:
choices: The cell sits at its resting potential
test.explain: Capacitive current is I = C·dV/dt, so it is zero when voltage is steady and appears whenever voltage changes.

test.q: The time for the membrane voltage to reach about 63% of its final value is written with the Greek letter ___.
test.explain: The time constant is written τ (tau) and equals Rm × Cm.

test.q: What is the name for the ratio ΔV/ΔI measured when current is injected into a whole cell?
test.explain: Input resistance tells you how much a given current changes the voltage. It is high in small cells and low in large ones.

test.q: In the equivalent circuit, each ion's ___ potential acts as a battery in series with its conductance.
test.explain: The reversal (equilibrium) potential, given by the Nernst equation, is the voltage at which that ion's net flow stops. This is why it works like a battery.

kidTest.q: In the bucket story, what do the tiny holes stand for?
kidTest.explain: The tiny holes are ion channels, which let charge leak out of the cell.

kidTest.q: What happens when you stop pouring water into the bucket?
kidTest.explain: Without new water coming in, the water slowly leaks out through the holes, just as charge leaks out of a cell.

kidTest.q: Does a cell's voltage jump up all at once?
kidTest.explain: The bucket has to fill up first, so the voltage rises bit by bit.

kidTest.q: What happens if the bucket has fewer holes?
choices: It shrinks to a smaller size
kidTest.explain: Fewer holes means less leaking, so the water (charge) stays in longer.

kidTest.q: The part that stores charge, like the bucket wall, is called a c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A capacitor stores charge. The cell's thin skin works like one.

advancedTest.q: Two compact neurons have identical specific Rm and Cm, but neuron B has four times the membrane area of neuron A. Compared with A, neuron B has:
choices: Same τ, four-fold higher input resistance
Four-fold longer τ, same input resistance
advancedTest.explain: Area cancels out of τ = Rm(Ω·cm²) × Cm(F/cm²), so τ is unchanged. Four times the area puts four times as many channels in parallel, which cuts input resistance to one quarter.

advancedTest.q: In vivo synaptic bombardment doubles a neuron's total membrane conductance (a high-conductance state). What follows for its passive integration?
choices: τ halves; inputs get smaller and briefer
Input resistance doubles while τ halves
τ doubles; inputs summate over longer windows
τ stays fixed because capacitance is fixed
advancedTest.explain: Doubling conductance halves resistance, so τ = RC halves and each input produces a smaller, shorter voltage change. Capacitance staying fixed does not keep τ constant, because R has changed.

advancedTest.q: In RC terms, why does wrapping an internode in many layers of myelin help an axon conduct?
choices: It lowers axial resistance in the axon core
It cuts capacitance and raises resistance
It raises capacitance to store more charge
It adds sodium channels along internodes
advancedTest.explain: Stacking membranes in series divides capacitance and multiplies resistance, so less charge is lost charging and leaking across the internode. Myelin does not change the axial resistance of the axon core.

advancedTest.q: A membrane has K+ conductance nine times its Na+ conductance (E_K = −90 mV, E_Na = +60 mV), with other ions ignored. Its steady-state voltage is about:
advancedTest.explain: By the chord conductance equation, V = (9 × −90 + 1 × 60)/10 = −75 mV. The voltage lies near E_K because K+ has the larger conductance, but it does not equal E_K.

lessons.title: Signals and Noise: Amplifiers, Sampling Rate, Nyquist and Filtering

levels.kid:
Imagine trying to hear a friend whisper at a loud party. The whisper is the **signal**: the part you want. The party sounds are the **noise**: everything else.

Brain cells send tiny electric whispers. Scientists use an **amplifier**, like a super-strong ear trumpet, to make them bigger. But it makes the noise bigger too, so scientists try to keep things quiet from the start.

Next, a computer takes snapshots of the signal, thousands of them every second. If it takes too few snapshots, fast wiggles get missed or look wrong. It is like a spinning wheel in a movie that seems to turn backwards.

Last, **filters** work like sieves. They keep the part of the signal you want and toss out the rest, like the buzz that comes from wall plugs.
levels.hs:
Every recording has two parts. The **signal** is the brain activity you care about. The **noise** is everything else. Scientists track the **signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**, which tells you how big the signal is compared to the noise.

Brain signals are tiny. A spike recorded just outside a neuron may be only around 100 microvolts (millionths of a volt). Scalp EEG waves are often 10 to 100 microvolts. So the first step is an **amplifier**, which multiplies the voltage, for example 1,000 times. That multiplying factor is its **gain**. Most recordings use **differential amplification**: the amplifier measures the difference between two electrodes. Noise that hits both electrodes equally, like electrical hum from wall power at 50 or 60 Hz, cancels out.

Next, a computer **samples** the signal, measuring it many times per second. The **Nyquist rule** says you must sample at more than twice the fastest frequency in the signal. Sample too slowly and you get **aliasing**: fast signals disguise themselves as slow ones, like car wheels that seem to spin backwards in a video.

Finally, **filters** remove unwanted frequencies:
- **Low-pass** keeps slow parts and removes fast noise.
- **High-pass** removes slow drift.
- **Notch** removes one frequency, like 60 Hz hum.

Real example: to record spikes, labs often sample about 30,000 times per second and keep frequencies from roughly 300 to 6,000 Hz.
levels.college:
Every method in this course runs the same pipeline: **transducer → amplifier → filter → analog-to-digital converter (ADC) → analysis**. Errors made early often cannot be undone later.

**Noise sources**
- **Thermal (Johnson) noise**: random motion of charge in any resistor. Its RMS voltage is √(4kTRB), so it rises with resistance R, temperature T and bandwidth B. A 1 MΩ electrode over a 10 kHz bandwidth at room temperature gives about 13 µV RMS.
- **Line noise**: mains interference at 50 Hz (Europe) or 60 Hz (Americas) plus harmonics. It is reduced with Faraday cages, careful grounding and avoiding ground loops.
- **1/f (flicker) noise**, which dominates at low frequencies.
- **Biological noise**: muscle (EMG), heartbeat (ECG), eye movements and background neural activity.

**Amplifiers.** Good front ends have high gain, very high **input impedance** (so they draw little current from a high-resistance electrode), and a high **common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR)**, often about 100 dB (100,000:1). The first stage, the **headstage**, sits close to the preparation so the tiny signal travels only a short distance before amplification.

**Sampling and Nyquist.** At sampling rate fs, the highest representable frequency is the **Nyquist frequency**, fs/2. Energy above it **aliases**, folding down to appear as a false lower frequency. Aliased energy is inseparable from real signal, so an analog **anti-aliasing low-pass filter** goes *before* the ADC. Because real filters roll off gradually, labs sample at several times the cutoff (for example, a 5 kHz filter with 20 to 50 kHz sampling in patch clamp).

**Digitization.** An N-bit ADC splits its range into 2^N levels; 16 bits gives 65,536. Amplify so the signal fills much of the range without clipping.

**Filters**
- Cutoff is the −3 dB point (amplitude about 71%).
- Each filter pole adds about 20 dB/decade of roll-off.
- **Bessel** filters preserve waveform shape; **Butterworth** filters have flatter passbands but overshoot and ring.
- Typical bands: spikes about 300 to 6,000 Hz; local field potentials (LFP) below about 300 Hz.
levels.phd:
**Sampling theory.** The Nyquist-Shannon theorem (Nyquist 1928; Shannon 1949; anticipated by Whittaker and Kotelnikov) states that a signal strictly band-limited below B is fully determined by samples taken at fs > 2B and can be reconstructed exactly by sinc interpolation. Neural signals are never strictly band-limited, so the guarantee is approximate and holds only if the analog anti-aliasing filter has pushed out-of-band power below the noise floor. Aliased components fold to |f − k·fs|: sampled at 1 kHz, a 900 Hz component appears at 100 Hz, indistinguishable from genuine activity.

**Quantization.** An ideal N-bit ADC adds uniform quantization noise of LSB/√12 RMS, giving a maximum SNR of about 6.02N + 1.76 dB (roughly 98 dB for 16 bits). Modern multichannel chips digitize at the headstage; the Intan RHD2000 family resolves 0.195 µV per bit.

**Noise in current measurement.** In a patch-clamp headstage, thermal current noise from the feedback resistor scales as √(4kTB/R), so gigaohm resistors give quieter low-frequency recordings. At higher frequencies, amplifier voltage noise acting across input and pipette capacitance dominates, so current noise density rises with frequency. That is why picoampere single-channel recordings are low-pass filtered at modest cutoffs (often 1 to 5 kHz), and why the low-noise gigaseal was transformative.

**Averaging.** For a time-locked signal in stationary, uncorrelated noise, averaging N trials improves amplitude SNR by √N: quadrupling trials halves residual noise. Dawson's averaging work in the early 1950s made evoked potentials measurable. Latency jitter, adaptation or correlated noise blur or bias the average.

**Filter-induced distortion, an ongoing debate**
- Causal filters impose frequency-dependent phase delay; Quian Quiroga (2009) showed this distorts extracellular spike shape, undermining cell-type classification by waveform width.
- Zero-phase (forward-backward) filtering removes delay but is non-causal, smearing activity backward in time; VanRullen (2011) warned this can make effects appear to begin earlier than they truly do.
- Overly aggressive high-pass filtering of ERPs can create artifactual opposite-polarity components (Tanner, Morgan-Short and Luck, 2015).
- Narrowband filtering of broadband noise produces rhythmic-looking output, so a filtered rhythm alone does not prove a true oscillation.
levels.expert:
**Fix the irreversible settings first.** Anti-aliasing cutoff, sampling rate, gain and reference cannot be corrected afterward, so choose them from the fastest feature you need. Neuropixels 1.0 probes show the modern solution: 960 sites with 384 selectable channels, digitized on the probe by 10-bit ADCs, with each channel split into an action-potential band sampled at 30 kHz and an LFP band at 2.5 kHz. Because digitization happens on the probe, microvolt analog signals never travel down long cables collecting interference.

**Aliasing beyond electrophysiology.** In fMRI, a repetition time (TR) of 2 s gives a Nyquist frequency of 0.25 Hz. Cardiac (about 1 Hz) and respiratory (about 0.3 Hz) fluctuations fold into the slow BOLD band used for resting-state connectivity. Remedies include physiological regression (such as RETROICOR) and multiband acquisitions with sub-second TRs.

**Operating room realities**
- Intraoperative monitoring averages hundreds of trials for somatosensory evoked potentials, while electrocautery and other OR equipment inject large broadband interference.
- In deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery, microelectrode recordings are band-passed for spikes and played as audio so the team can hear the electrode enter targets such as the subthalamic nucleus.
- Sensing DBS devices (Medtronic Percept) stream LFP at about 250 Hz during stimulation near 130 Hz. Stimulation and ECG artifacts must be rejected before beta-band (13 to 30 Hz) power can drive adaptive DBS, which the FDA approved in 2025.

**Pitfalls**
- Notch filters ring around sharp transients, and line harmonics (100/150 or 120/180 Hz) overlap high-gamma; spectral interpolation or line-noise regression is often gentler.
- Stimulation artifacts saturate amplifiers, and recovery or blanking periods hide early responses.
- A digital filter applied after sampling cannot undo aliasing; folded energy already sits in the band.
- Downsampling without low-pass filtering first re-creates aliasing.
- Methods sections should report filter type, order, cutoffs, and causal versus zero-phase; many still omit these.

**Open questions.** Implanted brain-computer interfaces generate more data than wireless links can carry, pushing toward on-chip spike detection and compression. How much decodable information lossy compression discards, and which features decoders truly need, remain active research questions.

keyPoints: SNR compares the size of the signal you want to the noise you don't
Differential amplifiers with high CMRR cancel noise shared by both inputs
Thermal noise grows with resistance, temperature and bandwidth
Sample faster than twice the highest frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing
The anti-aliasing low-pass filter goes before the ADC; aliasing can't be undone
Filters reshape signals: choose type, cutoff and phase behavior deliberately

test.q: You need to record activity up to 5,000 Hz. By the Nyquist rule, the minimum sampling rate is just above:
test.explain: Nyquist requires sampling at more than twice the highest frequency: 2 × 5,000 = 10,000 Hz. Labs often go higher in practice, but 10,000 Hz is the theoretical minimum.

test.q: What is aliasing in a sampled recording?
choices: Loss of signal when the amplifier clips
Slow drift added by electrode movement
Hum picked up from mains wiring
Fast signals posing as slower ones
test.explain: When sampling is too slow, frequencies above the Nyquist frequency fold down and appear as false lower frequencies. Drift and hum are different kinds of noise.

test.q: A differential amplifier reduces 60 Hz hum mainly because it:
choices: Cools the electrode to cut noise
Samples faster than the hum frequency
test.explain: It amplifies the difference between two electrodes, so interference that appears equally on both (common-mode) cancels. CMRR measures how well it does this.

test.q: To remove slow baseline drift while keeping spikes, you would use a:
test.explain: A high-pass filter passes high frequencies and blocks slow ones such as drift. A low-pass filter would do the opposite.

test.q: Why is the anti-aliasing filter placed before the analog-to-digital converter?
choices: Folded energy is permanent once sampled
It sets the number of bits in the ADC
It removes slow drift from the electrodes
It boosts amplifier gain before digitizing
test.explain: After sampling, aliased energy is mixed into the real band and can't be separated out, so high frequencies must be removed in analog form first.

test.q: Thermal (Johnson) noise increases when you increase:
test.explain: Thermal noise voltage is √(4kTRB), so it rises with resistance, temperature and bandwidth. Averaging more trials reduces noise instead.

test.q: A 16-bit ADC divides its input range into about how many levels?
test.explain: An N-bit converter has 2^N levels, and 2^16 = 65,536. 256 levels would be an 8-bit converter.

test.q: Which filter type is chosen when preserving the waveform's shape matters most?
test.explain: Bessel filters keep waveform shape with little overshoot. Butterworth filters have flatter passbands but overshoot and ring.

test.q: Which frequency band is typically kept for recording extracellular spikes?
test.explain: Spikes are brief, so their energy sits roughly between 300 and 6,000 Hz. Frequencies below about 300 Hz form the local field potential.

test.q: Half the sampling rate is called the ___ frequency.
test.explain: The Nyquist frequency (fs/2) is the highest frequency a given sampling rate can faithfully represent.

test.q: What type of filter removes one narrow frequency, such as 60 Hz mains hum?
test.explain: A notch (band-stop) filter removes a narrow band around one frequency, such as line noise.

test.q: An amplifier's ___ is the factor by which it multiplies the input voltage.
test.explain: Gain is the amplification factor. A gain of 1,000 turns 100 µV into 100 mV.

kidTest.q: In a brain recording, what is the 'noise'?
choices: The part you want to hear
kidTest.explain: Noise is everything except the signal you are trying to hear.

kidTest.q: What does an amplifier do?
kidTest.explain: An amplifier works like a strong ear trumpet. It makes small signals bigger.

kidTest.q: What can happen if the computer takes too few snapshots?
kidTest.explain: Too few snapshots can miss fast wiggles or make them look wrong, like a wheel that seems to spin backwards.

kidTest.q: A filter works a bit like a:
kidTest.explain: Like a sieve, a filter keeps the part you want and lets the rest go.

kidTest.q: Brain cells send tiny electric whispers. The part you want to hear is the s _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The signal is the part you want. Everything else is noise.

advancedTest.q: A recording is sampled at 1 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. Interference at 1,200 Hz would appear in the data at:
advancedTest.explain: Aliased components fold to |f − k·fs|: |1,200 − 1,000| = 200 Hz. 1,200 Hz itself is above the 500 Hz Nyquist frequency and can't be represented.

advancedTest.q: With an fMRI repetition time of 2 s, why does cardiac pulsation contaminate slow resting-state BOLD fluctuations?
choices: Heartbeat raises thermal noise in the receive coil
Pulsation adds 1/f noise to the BOLD baseline
Each heartbeat directly triggers a BOLD response
Its ~1 Hz rhythm is above Nyquist and folds down
advancedTest.explain: A 2 s TR samples at 0.5 Hz, giving a 0.25 Hz Nyquist frequency. The roughly 1 Hz cardiac signal aliases into the slow band used for connectivity.

advancedTest.q: An ERP average from 100 trials is still noisy. Under ideal conditions, about how many trials would halve the residual noise amplitude?
advancedTest.explain: SNR improves with √N, so halving noise needs four times the trials: 400. Doubling to 200 gives only about a 1.4-fold improvement.

advancedTest.q: A study filters EEG with a zero-phase filter and finds a response that seems to begin before the expected time. The most likely explanation is that:
choices: Non-causal filtering smeared activity backward in time
Quantization noise from the ADC shifted the baseline
The causal filter added a phase delay to the response
Line noise harmonics masked the true onset of the signal
advancedTest.explain: Forward-backward (zero-phase) filtering is non-causal, so it spreads activity both earlier and later in time, making onsets look early. A causal filter would delay the response, not advance it.

lessons.title: Experimental Logic: Observation, Perturbation and Causal Inference

levels.kid:
Imagine a rooster crows every morning, and then the sun comes up. Does the rooster make the sun rise? No! The two things just happen together. Scientists have to be careful not to mix up "happens together" with "makes it happen."

To study the brain, scientists first **watch**. This is called **observation**. They listen to brain cells or take pictures of the brain while it works.

Then they **change** something. This is called **perturbation**. They might gently turn off a tiny brain part for a while, or turn it on, and see what happens. If turning off a part stops a job, that part helps do that job.

The secret is a **fair test**. Change just one thing, and keep everything else the same.
levels.hs:
Neuroscience has two basic ways of learning how the brain works.

**Observation** means measuring the brain without changing it. Examples include recording electrical signals from neurons or scanning blood flow with fMRI. Observation shows **correlation**, meaning two things change together. But correlation is not **causation**. A brain area that lights up during fear might cause the fear. It might instead simply respond to the fear, which is called **reverse causation**. Or both might be driven by a third factor, called a **confound**.

**Perturbation** means deliberately changing the brain and watching what happens to behavior. Scientists can silence neurons with drugs or light, or stimulate them with electrical current. Perturbations answer two key questions:
- Is the area **necessary**? If you turn it off, does the behavior disappear?
- Is the area **sufficient**? If you turn it on, does the behavior appear?

Good experiments include a **control group** that gets everything except the key manipulation. Comparing against this group shows that the manipulation, and not something else, caused the effect.

A famous early example came from nature itself. In 1861, the French physician **Paul Broca** studied a patient nicknamed "Tan," because that was nearly the only word he could say. After the patient died, Broca found damage in the left frontal lobe. This "natural lesion" linked that region, now called Broca's area, to producing speech.
levels.college:
Most neuroscience claims follow a three-step logic:
- **Correlate**: record activity and show it tracks a stimulus or behavior.
- **Necessity (loss of function)**: remove or silence the activity and show the behavior is impaired.
- **Sufficiency (gain of function)**: drive the activity and show that the behavior, or a bias in it, appears.

**Perturbation tools** vary in precision. Lesions (surgical, stroke or toxin-induced) are permanent and coarse. Pharmacological inactivation, for example infusing the GABA-A agonist **muscimol**, is reversible over hours. Electrical **microstimulation** activates neurons near an electrode tip. **Optogenetics** and **chemogenetics** target genetically defined cell types. Optogenetics acts on a timescale of milliseconds, and chemogenetics over minutes to hours.

**Classic evidence.** In 1953, William Scoville removed most of patient **H.M.**'s medial temporal lobes, including much of both hippocampi, to treat his epilepsy. Brenda Milner showed that afterwards he could no longer form new long-term declarative memories, yet he could still learn motor skills such as mirror drawing. In 1990, **Salzman, Britten and Newsome** microstimulated clusters of direction-selective neurons in monkey area **MT** while the monkeys judged noisy motion. Stimulation biased their choices toward the neurons' preferred direction. Earlier recordings had shown that MT activity correlates with perception; stimulation showed that it can causally shape perception.

**Double dissociation.** In a single dissociation, lesion A impairs task 1 but not task 2. That result could simply mean task 1 is harder. A **double dissociation** is stronger evidence that two tasks depend on separable systems (Teuber, 1955). Here lesion A impairs task 1 but not task 2, and lesion B impairs task 2 but not task 1.

**Controls** must match everything except the variable of interest. Examples are sham surgery and vehicle injections. In optogenetics, a key control is animals that receive the same light but express no opsin, because light and heat alone can change behavior. Blinding and randomization reduce experimenter bias.

No single method is decisive. Confidence comes from **converging evidence** across observation and perturbation.
levels.phd:
Formally, observation estimates P(Y | X), whereas perturbation estimates P(Y | do(X)), in **Judea Pearl's** notation. The difference matters because conditioning on an observed X leaves all of X's upstream causes in play, so any common cause (a confound) leaks into the association. An intervention sets X externally and cuts it off from its usual causes in the causal graph. Any remaining change in Y must then flow through paths downstream of X. Randomization achieves the same severing at the level of treatment assignment, which is why randomized trials and well-controlled manipulations rank above observational studies.

Statistical shortcuts are weaker than they look. **Granger causality** is widely applied to EEG, LFP and fMRI time series. It tests whether the past of X improves prediction of Y, so it is predictive, not interventional. It is vulnerable to unmeasured common inputs and to differences in measurement lag, such as regional variation in the hemodynamic response.

Perturbation has its own pitfalls in distributed, recurrent, degenerate circuits:
- **Diaschisis** (von Monakow, 1914): damage to one region depresses function in distant regions that are connected but intact, so a deficit can be misattributed to the lesioned site.
- **Acute versus chronic effects**: Otchy and colleagues (Nature, 2015) found that transient inactivation in songbirds and rats disrupted behaviors that were spared or recovered after permanent lesions of the same region. This suggests that acute silencing can perturb connected circuits off-target rather than reveal a required computation.
- **Compensation and degeneracy**: several circuit configurations can produce the same output, so a null effect of silencing does not prove a region is uninvolved.
- **Unnatural sufficiency**: synchronous optogenetic drive of thousands of neurons may produce behavior through activity patterns the brain does not normally generate.

Jonas and Kording (2017) dramatized these limits. They applied standard neuroscience analyses to a simulated MOS 6502 microprocessor running video games. Lesioning single transistors identified some that abolished one game but not others, yet no transistor "encoded" that game. Tuning curves, connectivity analyses and dimensionality reduction likewise yielded plausible but misleading accounts.

Newsome's MT program remains the exemplar of combining approaches. Neurometric curves from single neurons rivaled psychometric performance (Newsome, Britten and Movshon, 1989). Choice-related fluctuations linked trial-by-trial activity to decisions, and microstimulation closed the causal loop.
levels.expert:
In practice, the weakest link in a causal claim is usually the control, not the manipulation.

**Optogenetics.** Owen, Liu and Kreitzer (Nature Neuroscience, 2019) showed that continuous light delivery of the kind commonly used in vivo can heat tissue by a few degrees Celsius. This heating suppressed firing of striatal neurons and produced rotational behavior even in opsin-free mice. Minimum safeguards include:
- fluorophore-only (for example eYFP) animals receiving identical light
- reporting of light power and duty cycle
- post hoc verification of expression and fiber placement

Inhibitory opsins add further complications. Prolonged activation of light-driven proton pumps such as ArchT can alter presynaptic pH and paradoxically increase transmitter release, and rebound firing can follow light offset.

**Chemogenetics.** Gomez and colleagues (Science, 2017) showed that clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) penetrates the brain poorly and is back-metabolized to **clozapine**. Clozapine crosses into the brain readily and binds both DREADDs and native dopamine, serotonin and other receptors. Every CNO experiment therefore needs ligand-treated, DREADD-free controls. Newer ligands such as **deschloroclozapine** (Nagai et al., 2020) reduce this concern but do not abolish it.

**Statistics as experimental logic.** Several common errors manufacture false causal claims:
- **Pseudoreplication**: treating cells or slices from one animal as independent samples (Lazic, 2010).
- **Double dipping**: selecting data with one analysis and testing it with a second analysis that is not independent (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009).
- **Uncorrected multiple comparisons**: famously illustrated by apparent "activation" in an fMRI scan of a dead salmon (Bennett et al.).

Many journals now expect preregistration, blinded scoring and power analysis.

**Operating room.** Neurosurgeons face the same logic. fMRI language maps are correlational: they show regions engaged during a task, not regions essential to it. **Direct cortical stimulation** during awake craniotomy acts as a reversible virtual lesion. Speech arrest at a site is the clinical gold standard for sparing that site, although afterdischarges spreading from the stimulated site can mislocalize function. **Lesion network mapping** (Boes, Fox and colleagues) uses connectome data to show that lesions causing the same symptom often share a network rather than a location.

**Frontier.** Two-photon holographic optogenetics can now activate chosen ensembles of a few dozen neurons. Marshel et al. (Science, 2019) stimulated orientation-specific ensembles in V1 and elicited behavior consistent with perceiving the stimulus. Two questions remain open. How close to natural activity must a perturbation be to count as evidence? And how can causality be inferred in circuits that adapt to the manipulation itself?

keyPoints: Observation reveals correlation; perturbation tests causation
Confounds and reverse causation can create false causal links
Silencing tests necessity; activating tests sufficiency
Double dissociations show two functions rely on separable systems
Controls (sham, vehicle, light-only, ligand-only) must match everything except the manipulation
Perturbations have pitfalls: off-target acute effects, diaschisis, compensation

test.q: A rooster crows every morning just before sunrise. Concluding that crowing causes sunrise confuses:
test.explain: The two events happen together (correlation), but one does not produce the other (causation).

test.q: Which approach is a perturbation rather than an observation?
test.explain: Silencing deliberately changes brain activity. Recording, fMRI and calcium imaging measure activity without changing it.

test.q: Silencing region X abolishes behavior Y. This tests whether X is:
test.explain: A loss-of-function experiment asks whether the behavior still happens without X, which is a test of necessity. Sufficiency would require activating X.

test.q: Stimulating region X produces behavior Y in a resting animal. This is evidence that X is:
test.explain: A gain-of-function result, where driving X makes Y appear, tests sufficiency. It does not show that Y needs X.

test.q: Patient A has damage to area 1 and loses face recognition but not reading. Patient B has damage to area 2 and loses reading but not face recognition. This pattern is a:
test.explain: Each lesion impairs one task and spares the other, in opposite directions. That rules out a simple difficulty explanation and suggests separable systems.

test.q: The possibility that the effect produces the supposed cause, rather than the other way round, is called:
test.explain: In reverse causation, a brain area active during fear might be responding to the fear rather than causing it.

test.q: Patient H.M. lost the ability to form new long-term memories after surgery removed much of his:
choices: Prefrontal cortex in both frontal lobes
Visual cortex in both occipital lobes
test.explain: Scoville removed most of H.M.'s medial temporal lobes, including much of both hippocampi. His motor skill learning was spared.

test.q: Microstimulating motion-tuned neurons in monkey area MT while monkeys judged noisy motion caused them to:
choices: Forget the rules of the task
Lose vision in the opposite eye
test.explain: Salzman, Britten and Newsome (1990) found that stimulation biased the monkeys' choices toward the stimulated neurons' preferred direction. This showed that MT activity causally shapes motion perception.

test.q: Why do optogenetics experiments include animals that receive light but express no opsin?
choices: To check effects of illumination alone
To measure which light color works best
To make the neurons fire faster
To increase the size of the effect
test.explain: Light and heat alone can change neural activity and behavior. Opsin-free animals receiving identical light reveal these non-specific effects.

test.q: A third factor that drives both the supposed cause and the effect, creating a false link between them, is called a ___.
test.explain: Confounds create correlations without a direct causal link. Perturbation and randomization help break them.

test.q: Which French physician linked the left frontal lobe to speech production after studying a patient nicknamed "Tan" in 1861?
test.explain: Paul Broca found left frontal damage in Tan's brain. The region is now called Broca's area.

test.q: The group that receives everything except the key manipulation is called the ___ group.
test.explain: A control group lets you attribute any difference to the manipulation itself rather than to other factors.

kidTest.q: The rooster crows, then the sun comes up. Does the rooster make the sun rise?
choices: Yes, the crowing pulls it up
No, it is just good timing
Yes, the sun listens for it
kidTest.explain: The two things happen together, but the rooster does not make the sun rise.

kidTest.q: What is it called when scientists just watch the brain without changing it?
kidTest.explain: Observation means watching and measuring without changing anything.

kidTest.q: To learn what a brain part does, scientists can change it. What is one way?
choices: Look at it from far away
Turn it off for a while
kidTest.explain: Gently turning a part off shows what jobs it helps with. Looking and drawing do not change it.

kidTest.q: In a fair test, how many things should you change at once?
kidTest.explain: If you change just one thing, you know that thing caused what happened.

kidTest.q: When you change just one thing and keep everything else the same, it is a f _ _ _ test.
kidTest.explain: A fair test changes one thing at a time.

advancedTest.q: Muscimol inactivation of a region abolishes a learned behavior, but the behavior is intact days after a permanent lesion of the same region. The most cautious interpretation is:
choices: Acute silencing may disrupt connected circuits off-target
Muscimol is a weak blocker of neural activity here
The region stores the behavior and quickly regrows
Permanent lesions are less complete than drug inactivation
advancedTest.explain: Otchy et al. (2015) showed that transient inactivation can perturb downstream circuits and produce deficits that do not reflect a required role. A strong acute effect argues against muscimol being weak.

advancedTest.q: Why does an intervention, do(X), support causal conclusions that conditioning on an observed X does not?
choices: It boosts the statistical power of the data
It makes X and Y independent by design
It cuts X off from its usual upstream causes
It measures X with less instrument noise
advancedTest.explain: Setting X externally severs the arrows into X, so confounds can no longer create the association. Any remaining change in Y must flow downstream of X.

advancedTest.q: Lesioning single transistors in a simulated microprocessor abolished one video game but not others. The lesson for neuroscience is that:
choices: Microprocessors are a poor model of anything
Lesion effects can mislead about a part's function
Each transistor encodes one specific game
Necessity tests are more reliable than recordings
advancedTest.explain: Jonas and Kording found that no transistor "encoded" a game. A selective lesion deficit therefore does not show that a component represents the lost function.

advancedTest.q: A DREADD study compares CNO with vehicle in DREADD-expressing mice but includes no CNO-treated DREADD-free mice. The main concern is that:
choices: The receptor may respond too slowly to the ligand
Its metabolite clozapine acts on native receptors
Vehicle injections may be too stressful to compare
Viral expression may reach too few target cells
advancedTest.explain: CNO is back-metabolized to clozapine, which binds native receptors. Behavioral effects could therefore occur without DREADDs. Vehicle controls do not address this, but ligand-treated DREADD-free mice do.
